# Getting Started

## Installing of required packages

|  |  |
|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| ggridges | ggplot extension for plotting ridgeline plots |
| ggdist | ggplot extension for visualising distribution and uncertainty |
| tidyverse | a family of modern R packages specially designed to support data science, analysis and communication task including creating static statistical graphs |
| ggthemes | ggplot extension that provides the user additional themes, scales and geoms for the ggplots package |
| colorspace | R package provides a broad toolbox for selecting individual colors or color palettes, manipulating these colors and employing them in various kinds of visualisations |

: {tbl-colwidths="\[15,85\]"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(ggdist, ggridges, ggthemes,
               colorspace, tidyverse)
```
:::


## Importing data

For this exercise, Exam_data.csv will be used.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
exam <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")
```
:::


# Visualising Distribution with Ridgeline Plot

Ridgeline plot (sometimes called Joyplot) is a data visualisation technique for revealing the distribution of a numeric value for several groups. Distribution can be represented using histograms or density plots, all aligned to the same horizontal scale and presented with a slight overlap.

::: callout-note
-   Ridgeline plots make sense when the number of group to represent is medium to high, and thus a classic window separation would take to much space. Indeed, the fact that groups overlap each other allows to use space more efficiently. If you have less than 5 groups, dealing with other distribution plots in a probably better.
-   It works well when there is a clear pattern in the result, like if there is an obvious ranking in groups. Otherwise group will tend to overlap each other, leading to a messy plot not providing any insight.
:::

## Plotting ridgeline graph using ggridges method

There are several ways to plot ridgeline plot with R. In this section, you will learn how to plot ridgeline plot by using [ggridges](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/index.html) package.

ggridges package provides two main geom to plot gridgeline plots, they are [geom_ridgeline()](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_ridgeline.html) and [geom_density_ridges()](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/geom_density_ridges.html). The former takes height values directlly to draw the ridgelines, and the latter first estimates data densitites and then draws those using ridgelines.

The code chunk below uses `geom_density_ridges()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white") +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Varying fill colors along the x-axis

Sometimes we would like to have the area under a ridgeline not filled with a single solid color but rather with colors that vary in some form along the x-axis. This effect can be achieved by using either geom_ridgeline_gradient() or geom_density_ridges_gradient(). Both geoms work just like `geom_ridgeline()` and `geom_density_ridges()`, except that they allow for varying fill colors. However, they do not allows for alpha transparency in the fill. For technical reasons, we can can eave changing fill colors or transpoarency but not both.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Score",
                      option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous( name = "English grades", 
                      expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Mapping the probabilities directly onto color

Besides providing additional geom objects to support the need to plot ridgeline plot, ggridges package also provides a stat function called [stat_density_ridges()](https://wilkelab.org/ggridges/reference/stat_density_ridges.html) that replaces [stat_density()](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html) of ggplot.

The code chunk is plotted by mapping the probabilities calculated using `stat(ecdf)` which represent the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-important
It is important to include argument `calc_scdf = TRUE` in `stat_density_ridges()`.
:::

## Ridgeline plots with quantile lines

By using geom_density_ridges_gradients(), we can colour the ridgeline plot by quantile, via the calculated stat(quantile) aesthetic as shown in the code chunk below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
                      quantiles = 4,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Instead of using number to define the quantiles, we can also specify quantiles by cut points such as 2.5% and 97.5% tails to color the ridgeline plot as shown in the figure below.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
                      quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


# Visualising Distribution with Raincloud Plot

Raincloud Plot is a data visualisation technique that produces a half-density to a distribution plot. It gets the name because the density plot is in the shape of a raincloud. The raincloud (half-density) plot enhances the tradition box-plot by highlighting multiple modalities (an indicator that groups may exist). The boxplot does not show where densities are clustered, by the raincloud plot does.

## Plotting a half eye graph

Plot Half-eye graph using [stat_halfeye()](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/reference/stat_halfeye.html) of ggdist package.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-tip
### Things to learn from code chunk

We remove the slab interval by setting `.width = 0` and `point_colour = NA`.
:::

## Adding the boxplot with `geom_boxplot()`

Next, add second geometry layer using `geom_boxplot()` of ffplot. This produces a narrow boxplot. We reduce the width and adjust the opacity.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Adding Dot Plots with `stat_dots()`

Next, add third geometry layer using [stat_dors()](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/reference/stat_dots.html) of ggdist package. This produces a half-dotplot, which is similar to a histogram that indicates the number of samples in each bin. We select side = "left" to inidicate we want it on the left-hand side.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Finishing touch

Lastly, `coord_flip()` of ggplot package will be used to flip the raincloud chart horizontally to give it the raincloud appearance. At the same time, `theme_economist()` of ggthmes package is used to give the raincloud chart a professional publishing standard look.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex4_p1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::
